Private Sector Investment in Sustainable Energy
M4: Financing Just Energy Transition
Lesson 1 Overview
In this lesson, learners will examine the role of private sector investment in driving the growth of renewable energy projects.
It covers the factors that attract private capital to the sector, such as technological advancements, revenue streams, policy incentives, and market potential.
The lesson also addresses barriers to private sector investment, particularly in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDE’s), and explores strategies to overcome these challenges.
By the end of this lesson, learners will understand the crucial role that private companies and investors play in scaling up sustainable energy projects globally.
Key Concepts
Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.
blended finance

Blended finance is a financial approach that combines public or philanthropic funds with private investment to support projects that have social or environmental benefits, aiming to attract more capital to achieve sustainable development goals.
cost of capital
The cost of capital is the return rate that a company must earn on its investments to satisfy its investors or creditors.

M4: Financing Just Energy Transition
A: Why is Private Sector Investment Essential for Advancing Sustainable Energy?

The need and role of private sector investment in sustainable energy has never been more critical as the world faces the challenge of addressing climate change, closing the existing investment gap and meeting growing energy demands needed to comply with the Paris Agreement.

Despite record-breaking public commitments, such as the new $300 billion annual climate finance target set at COP29 by 2035, the funding gap for achieving global clean energy transition goals remains vast.
According to IEA, reaching net-zero emissions by 2050 will require annual clean energy investments of over $4 trillion by the early 2030s.
One organization, the Global Renewables Alliance (GRA) objective is to triple global renewable energy capacity by 2030, reaching at least 11,000 gigawatts (GW).
This ambitious target aligns with the commitments made by world governments at COP28 in 2023.

To realize this goal, the GRA engages with governments, industry leaders, investors, non-governmental organizations, multilateral organizations, and corporations to accelerate the deployment of mobilizing finance for renewable energy technologies.

Furthermore, as technological advancements like green hydrogen, energy storage 💬️, and smart grids emerge, private investors bring not only capital but also expertise and best practices in scaling these solutions globally.
The private sectors involvement is key to transforming energy markets, fostering innovation, and ensuring that sustainable energy becomes accessible and affordable for all.
Private sector investment in sustainable energy has reached unprecedented levels, underscoring a global commitment to transitioning towards cleaner energy sources.
In 2024, global energy investment is projected to exceed USD 3 trillion for the first time, with USD 2 trillion directed towards clean energy technologies and infrastructure.
This surge is evident across various sectors.

For instance, private equity and venture capital investments in battery energy storage systems, energy management, and energy storage reached $17.86 billion by August 2024, already surpassing the total of $16.17 billion for the entire previous year.
Regionally, the United Kingdom has seen a significant influx of private equity and venture capital investment in the renewables sector, attracting $7.96 billion in the first nine months of 2024.
This surpasses the combined total of the previous four years and exceeds investments in the U.S.
renewables sector during the same period.
Overall these investments, though promising, are not sufficient to modernize aging grids and scale renewable energy systems globally.

For instance, the IEA notes that annual grid investment needs to triple to over $1 trillion annually by 2030 to support clean energy deployment and ensure energy security (IEA). For instance, as seen in the figure, the IEA estimates that grid investment needs to rise to
USD 820 billion by 2030, and USD 1 trillion in 2040 globally, before falling back after electricity is fully
decarbonised and the growth of renewables slows to match demand growth (IEA).
These latter countries will account for almost 45% of the average incremental investment needs from now to 2030, but the progress are still falling behind, especially Sub-Saharan Africa.

For 2035, estimates towards global investment requirements for climate action to be around $7– 8.1 trillion per year, with advanced economies needing $2.6–3.1 trillion, China $1.3–1.5 trillion, and EMDEs other than China requiring $3.1–3.5 trillion (IHLEG, 2024).

Although China is championing renewable energy investments, it is also important to address that they continue to be a large investor in new coal power construction.
In these regions, where energy access and poverty reduction are critical, the lack of adequate private sector involvement threatens to widen the gap in achieving sustainable development goals (SDGs).
Private sector investment in energy infrastructure from 2010 to 2020 highlights a promising shift toward renewable energy and supporting infrastructure.

Renewable energy generation attracted the largest share of private investment, reaching nearly $80 billion annually during this period, with only a modest 5% decline in 2020 despite the economic challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

However, while this stability underscores investor confidence and the sector’s central role in <ai prompt="Share details about decarbonization.">decarbonization 💬️</ai>, it still falls short of the levels required to keep pace with the urgent demands of the energy transition.
Meanwhile, investments in non-renewable energy generation declined sharply, with a 31% drop in 2020 rather than reflecting a global pivot away from fossil fuels.

While this decline aligns with increasing environmental awareness, targeted policy support and rapidly falling technology costs and stricter regulations, it underscores the urgent need to replace fossil fuel-based systems with renewable alternatives at a much faster rate.

Despite the progress in shifting capital toward renewables, emerging markets and developing economies (EMDE) —outside China—continue to lag in attracting private investment as mentioned in the previous lesson.

However, the needs and opportunities are especially significant in EMDE’s other than China as they are the countries that will account for the largest share of the increase in investments needed for a global energy transition as they are the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

Estimates points towards that the global projected investment requirement for climate action is around $6.3–6.7 trillion per year by 2030, of which $2.7–2.8 trillion is in advanced economies, $1.3-$1.4 trillion in China, and $2.3–2.5 trillion in EMDCs other than China (IHLEG, 2024).
Despite this significant increase in private sector investment a persistent finance gap remains, particularly in developing countries.
While global clean energy investment surpassed $2 trillion annually in 2024, less than 15% of this flows into emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) outside of China.

This disparity underscores a critical issue: the regions most vulnerable to climate change and in dire need of energy infrastructure receive only a fraction of the resources required to meet their sustainable energy needs.

Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 will require annual clean energy investments of $4 trillion per year by the early 2030s.
However, in developing countries, clean energy investment needs to increase more than sevenfold, from around $150 billion annually today to over $1 trillion by 2030.
Sub-Saharan Africa exemplifies this challenge, where over 600 million people still lack access to electricity.
Despite being rich in renewable energy potential, the region attracts only a small portion of global renewable energy investments.

For instance, in 2022, total clean energy investment in Africa was less than $25 billion and only went to a few countries, representing only 2% of global clean energy spending, despite the continent accounting for 17% of the global population.

Similarly, in South Asia, parts of Southeast Asia and Central Asia, investments remain insufficient to address the growing energy demands of rapidly urbanizing populations.
Without a significant increase in investment, these regions risk being locked into carbon-intensive energy systems or facing prolonged energy poverty.

B: Barriers To Private Sector Investment In Sustainable Energy
Part 2 Overview

Addressing the key bottlenecks that hinder private investors from targeting sectors and countries in need of additional investment is crucial for achieving the SDGs, energy transition and net-zero goals.
In this part we will discuss the four primary obstacles that hinder the private sector from investing in emerging and frontier markets, with the first being the most important
When it comes to barriers you can distinguish between two types of barriers: financial and non-financial:
Financial barriers:
Financial barriers include factors related to macroeconomic stability, such as currency volatility, inflation, taxes, and duties.

They also encompass the financial stability of off-takers, the liquidity of <ai prompt="Share details about energy markets.">energy markets 💬️</ai>, and other economic conditions that impact investment and project viability.
Non-financial barriers:
Pertain to aspects such as political stability, governance, and the rule of law.
These also include policies and regulations, institutional capacities, and other structural or administrative challenges that can hinder the successful implementation of energy projects.

Another important aspect in non-financial barriers is also the development of a local skilled workforce and human capital in energy transition projects and piloting new business models, addressing skill shortages and improving conditions for project implementation.
Financial Return Risk:
Private capital providers seek to maximize returns and safeguard capital as part of their fiduciary duty.

Although various investment opportunities in emerging and frontier markets could have a significant development impact, many transactions fail to meet investor return expectations relative to the risk.

Investors in emerging markets are exposed to specific risks such as business model risks related to new markets and projects, technical feasibility, macroeconomic and corporate governance risks, and funding shortages.

Furthermore, the expenses and time required can be significant to understand new markets, which is compounded by the capital-intensive nature of projects and the relatively small deals, reducing anticipated returns.
The challenge is to decrease the perceived and actual risk levels or to enhance the returns.
Inefficient markets:
Financial markets in emerging and frontier economies are typically less developed compared to those in developed countries.
They frequently do not have the necessary infrastructure, expertise, financial resources, and smooth supply-to-demand connection needed for efficient operation.

Bond and equity markets in less developed economies specifically are frequently underdeveloped and illiquid leading to significant uncertainty regarding investors' ability to exit the investment and recover their funds.
Institutional investors typically demand investment managers to possess a proven track record of favorable returns.
However, numerous local fund managers lack the necessary experience to showcase their performance as they are new to the industry.
Only a few financial institutions possess the necessary expertise to create tailored financial and non-financial solutions suitable for high-potential development sectors and countries.
The lack of scalable, liquid, standardized, and investable products hinders the efficient connection of capital supply and demand, and access to capital markets.

Cost of Capital:
One of the significant barriers impeding private sector investment in EMDE’s is the cost of capital.
Investors and financiers scrutinize the risks associated with investment projects in these regions, often demanding higher returns to compensate for perceived uncertainties.
EMDE’s frequently exhibit higher levels of political, regulatory, and economic risks compared to developed economies, leading to elevated capital costs.
These heightened costs diminish the attractiveness of investment opportunities, as they can erode potential returns and increase the threshold for profitability.

Consequently, private sector investors may be deterred from allocating capital to emerging markets, exacerbating the challenge of mobilizing adequate funding for essential development initiatives in these regions.

Efforts to mitigate the cost of capital through risk-mitigation strategies, regulatory reforms, and targeted incentives are essential to incentivize private sector involvement and unlock the economic potential of emerging markets.

The high cost of capital is often a result of various investment barriers and in some cases it may not represent a problem if there is adequate revenue generation is generated by a project.
In such cases, investors may still find opportunities viable despite higher financing expenses.

However, when revenue generation is uncertain or insufficient, the high cost of capital can deter private sector investment, making it harder to mobilize funding for essential development initiatives.

Addressing these challenges through risk-mitigation strategies, regulatory reforms, and targeted incentives can help enhance investment feasibility and unlock economic potential in emerging markets.
Difficult Local Investment Climates:
The absence of robust and transparent local regulatory and legal frameworks in EMDE’s hinders the inflow of private capital.
Capital controls, tax barriers, labor policies, inconsistent tariffs, and visa challenges hinder investment attractiveness by increasing transaction complexity and impeding return realization.
The limiting factors are exacerbated by risks related to fluctuating exchange rates, transaction complexity and operational risks, and political instability.
Regulatory policies in developed markets have impacted the ability of their private capital providers to conduct transactions in emerging and frontier economies.
Since 2008, numerous global banks have decreased their operations in EMDE’s due to stricter policies that have increased the expenses associated with long-term and high-risk lending.
Unintentionally, these policies have led to a lack of capital in important sectors such as infrastructure, clean energy, and local currency lending.

In addition, there is also a lack of capacity such as weak policy or regulatory frameworks and limited technical capacity for the preparation of bankable, investable, and financeable transformative projects, which poses a significant barrier to scaling up sustainable investments.

C: Scaling Up Private Sector investment
Part 3 Overview
Addressing the bottlenecks that hinder private investors from targeting sectors and countries in need of additional investment is crucial for achieving the SDGs and net-zero goals.
Here are three primary obstacles that hinder the private sector from investing in EMDE’s.
Maximizing Profitability while Mitigating Risks:
Investments in clean energy are increasingly crucially seen as both profitable and strategic by the private sector.
Companies and financial institutions recognize the economic opportunities in the savings, new technologies, and products that emerge from the decarbonization effort.

The expectation of a significant allocation of funds towards clean energy development, potentially reaching up to $20 trillion globally in the coming decade, underscores the private sector's pivotal role in the energy transition.
In 2023, low-emissions power, primarily from renewable sources like solar, is expected to account for almost 90% of the total new investment in electricity generation.

Specifically, solar investments were projected to surpass $1 billion per day, reaching $380 billion for the year, marking a significant milestone by edging spending above that in upstream oil for the first time.

The private sector's interest in clean energy investment is partly driven by the potential for profit and economic interest in a growing market, and due to regulatory compliance, but also because of concerns with private firms’ own sustainability and carbon profiles and Net Zero pledges and sustainability commitments.
Governments alone lack the financial capacity to drive the global clean energy transition at the required scale and tempo.
Hence the private sector's engagement is crucial .
Creating an Enabling Policy and Regulatory Environment:
Government policies and incentives can play a significant role in encouraging private investment in clean energy.
Policies aimed at reducing the risks associated with clean energy projects and improving their return on investment can significantly influence private sector decisions.

This includes tax incentives, subsidies for zero-emissions energy projects, and policies designed to ensure a stable market for clean energy.

For instance, initiatives like the US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) have spurred a wave of investment by providing incentives for renewable energy and other clean energy sectors such as electric vehicles, CCUS, and low-carbon hydrogen among others.

This policy-driven approach has initiated a global race to offer attractive investment opportunities in the renewable sector, further catalyzed by the development of local supply chains in the US and Europe and the expansion of China's supply chains.
It also offers the potential to help drive down costs for clean energy systems worldwide.
Leveraging Macroeconomic Conditions for Investment Growth:
During periods of economic expansion, companies are more likely to invest in new projects, including clean energy, due to higher expected returns.
In contrast, during economic downturns, investment tends to slow as companies become more risk-averse, focusing on conserving cash rather than expanding operations.
Macroeconomic conditions are a critical factor in the decision-making process for private sector investments in clean energy.
They not only determine the cost and availability of capital but also influence the overall risk-return profile of such projects.

As such, understanding these conditions is essential for stakeholders in the renewable energy sector to navigate the complexities of financing and investing in sustainable energy solutions.

Low interest rates can make borrowing cheaper, encouraging private companies to invest in clean energy projects, which are often capital-intensive and require a significant upfront investment.
Conversely, high interest rates can deter investment by increasing the cost of borrowing.
Therefore, central banks' monetary policies, which determine interest rates, play a crucial role in shaping the investment landscape for clean energy.

Moreover, inflation can have a dual effect – on the one hand increasing the cost of materials and labor for clean energy projects, making them more expensive to develop, while on the other hand, clean energy can be seen as a future hedge against inflation, especially if traditional energy sources become more expensive due to rising commodity prices.
Driving Investment through Technological Advancements and Cost Reductions:
The reduction in technology costs has been a pivotal driver for the surge in private sector investment in clean energy.

This trend is largely attributed to advancements in technology, economies of scale, and increased competition among manufacturers, leading to more accessible and affordable solutions.

Technological innovations have significantly improved the efficiency and effectiveness of renewable energy and other clean energy systems.

For instance, improvements in solar photovoltaic (PV) cell efficiency have allowed for greater electricity generation from the same amount of sunlight, reducing the cost per unit of electricity produced.

Similarly, advancements in wind turbine technology, including taller turbines with larger rotor diameters, have enabled access to higher wind speeds and more consistent generation, improving the economics of wind energy 💬️.

As the renewable energy market has expanded, manufacturers have been able to achieve economies of scale, reducing the per-unit cost of renewable energy technologies.
This is particularly evident in the solar PV and wind sectors, where large-scale production has led to significant cost reductions over the past decade.
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s electricity sector has historically relied on coal and hydropower as its primary sources of electricity generation, as shown in Figure 1.
While these sources ensured a domestic supply, they have created vulnerabilities, as hydropower is highly seasonal.

Meanwhile, coal-fired plants have contributed to Bosnia and Herzegovina having the world’s fifth-highest air pollution mortality rate (<a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/08/29/bosnia-and-herzegovina-deadly-air-pollution-killing-thousands"><u>Human Rights Watch, 2022, para.

This has limited the country’s ability to reduce its carbon footprint and meet its international climate obligations, including as a signatory to the Energy Community Treaty and its commitments under the Paris Agreement.
At the time, Bosnia and Herzegovina had not developed alternative renewable energy sources to diversify its electricity mix.
Despite strong wind potential in elevated and mountainous regions, wind energy remained largely untapped.

This lack of energy diversification was due to a combination of structural barriers, including limited experience with utility-scale wind projects and the absence of robust legal and regulatory frameworks to support their development.
The lack of operational wind farms and an enabling environment also discouraged private sector investment, hindering progress toward energy diversification.
Given these challenges, the Mesihovina Wind Farm was delivered through a structured partnership between public and private actors.

KfW Development Bank, the German state-owned development financier, provided a EUR 71 million concessional loan to Elektroprivreda HZ HB (EPHZHB), Bosnia and Herzegovina’s public utility responsible for implementation <a href="https://seenews.com/news/germanys-kfw-lends-71-mln-euro-for-bosnias-first-wind-farm-project-941471"><u>(SeeNews, 2010, para.

The German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development also provided additional funding, reflecting Germany’s broader commitment to supporting renewable energy and climate mitigation in the Western Balkans.
EPHZHB led project management, grid integration, and coordination with domestic institutions.

At the same time, Siemens Gamesa—a global private-sector leader in wind turbine technology—was contracted to supply and install 22 turbines, marking its first engagement in the Balkans <a href="https://renews.biz/43524/siemens-makes-balkans-debut/"><u>(Renews, 2016, para.
The partnership combined concessional public financing with private technical expertise and commercial delivery models.

With support from KfW and international consultants, EPHZHB collaborated with national authorities to align environmental and social safeguards with international norms and share knowledge on the technical nature of wind farm approval processes with government representatives <a href="https://www.kfw-entwicklungsbank.de/PDF/Evaluierung/Ergebnisse-und-Publikationen/PDF-Dokumente-A-D_EN/BosnienH_Mesihovina_2022_E.pdf"><u>(KfW, 2022, p.

This collaboration not only enabled successful project delivery but also strengthened institutional capacity and helped establish a more investable regulatory environment for future private sector participation in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s renewable energy sector.
The project followed a phased implementation process.
Feasibility studies identified Tomislavgrad as a suitable location due to favorable wind conditions and accessible terrain.
Once the site was selected, the project team developed legal and permitting procedures, including environmental and social impact assessments, in coordination with national authorities.

Following regulatory approvals, Siemens Gamesa was contracted to supply and install 22 SWT-2.3-108 turbines (<a href="https://www.rechargenews.com/wind/bosnia-and-herzegovina-enters-wind-power-era/2-1-296816"><u>Recharge News, 2018, para.

Despite logistical and weather-related challenges, the project was completed within budget, demonstrating the feasibility of mobilizing private sector expertise and technology in a market with no prior experience in utility-scale wind energy.

The project delivered several important results:

Installed 50.6 MW of wind capacity, generating an estimated 165 GWh annually, enough to supply approximately 27,500 households (Power Technology, 2024, para.

1, 3).
Avoided over 150,000 tons of CO₂ emissions annually (KfW, 2022, p.

8).
Demonstrated Bosnia and Herzegovina’s capacity to attract private sector investment and expertise in renewable energy infrastructure.
Strengthened institutional capacity within EPHZHB to manage complex renewable energy projects (KfW, 2022, p.
Contributed to creating an enabling environment for future renewable energy investments by supporting the development of regulatory and planning procedures (KfW, 2022, p.

4, 11).

The Mesihovina Wind Farm offers key lessons for similar contexts:

The importance of combining concessional finance with private sector technology partners to enable projects in markets with no prior track record.
The need for early regulatory and permitting framework development to prevent delays and increase investor confidence is essential.
The demonstration effect of flagship projects can catalyze broader market development, helping to attract further private-sector investment.
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s experience offers a replicable model for other Western Balkan countries, such as Serbia, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, that remain heavily dependent on coal.
It demonstrates how targeted investment and public-private collaboration can support energy diversification and emissions reduction in line with EU climate policy goals.
Key Takeaways
Public finance alone cannot meet the $4 trillion annual clean energy investment needed by 2030.
Private sector involvement is essential to scale innovations, accelerate renewable energy deployment, and achieve cost efficiencies globally.
While private sector investment in clean energy is increasing globally, developing countries lag significantly.
These regions attract less than 15% of global clean energy investments despite their high renewable energy potential and urgent energy access needs.
High financial risks, underdeveloped markets, high capital costs, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate infrastructure hinder private sector investment in sustainable energy.
However, solutions like risk mitigation tools, blended finance, regulatory reforms, and infrastructure development can unlock its potential.
